abstract: Our study examines the impact of the European Monetary Union (EMU) accession and convergence process on female labor force participation (FLFP) rates among women aged 25–54 in member countries. We employ the synthetic control framework to build a counterfactual for each member country, a composite of non‐EMU countries that mirrors its economic characteristics before the treatment year of 1995. By comparing actual post‐EMU FLFP rates with those of their synthetic counterparts, we estimate the causal effect of this process. We find substantial heterogeneity across member countries, with the strongest evidence concentrated in a small number of cases. Our results indicate a positive and economically meaningful influence on FLFP in the Netherlands. Ireland also exhibits a large positive posttreatment FLFP gap, although its weaker pretreatment fit warrants interpreting the Irish result as suggestive rather than conclusive. For the remaining members, differences between observed and synthetic FLFP are generally positive but are not consistently robust across placebo tests. Drawing insights from the literature, we also analyze the macroeconomic characteristics associated with the estimated FLFP gaps, providing additional context for our results.
title:
(Any) Female Labor Force Participation Effect of
                    EMU
                    Membership? Causal Inference Using the Synthetic Control Method

abstract: We follow the approach in Autor et al. to identify the effects of the US–China trade war on Mexico's local labor markets. We assess its effects on aggregate employment and wage levels and on the relative prices of skilled and unskilled labor. We find that, up to 2023, this shock has apparently led to an increase in the relative demand for unskilled labor and, thus, seems to have increased employment levels and unskilled wages, while reducing earnings of skilled workers. These effects were stronger in the border region of the country. The decline in the skill premium is consistent with the Stolper–Samuelson benchmark, although other mechanisms can generate similar responses.

abstract: Many governments aim to achieve equity in contracting—meaning that all firms, especially those considered disadvantaged, have an equal opportunity to compete. The same governments often measure success by the diversity in awards, determined by how frequently any disadvantaged firm wins. By extending a statistical discrimination model to a contracting setting, I show that buyers can treat ex ante similar disadvantaged firms differently, suggesting that award diversity may not translate into equitable opportunity for all disadvantaged firms. The model generates distinctive, strategic incentives between firms and highlights various challenges to achieving equity in contracting.
title: Diversity Versus Equity in Government Contracting

abstract: This paper explores how compulsory education laws shape occupational persistence in US agriculture. Using US Decennial Census data from 1860 to 1910, I examine occupational choices among adult children from farm households. I find that compulsory education reduces the probability of remaining in farming by 4%–7%. Event study estimates show that firstborn sons and White children are more likely to persist in agriculture. In contrast, daughters, non‐firstborn sons, and Black children are more likely to leave farming. Using the push–pull framework, I show that compulsory education affects occupational persistence through farm succession norms and expanded opportunities for off‐farm employment. Overall, the results help explain the under‐representation of women and Black Americans in US agriculture.
title:
Compulsory education and occupational persistence in
                    US
                    agriculture

abstract: A sender who wants a receiver to acquire items regardless of quality cannot communicate credibly about one item, but with several she can, by recommending weakly better items. We characterise a continuum of selective recommendation equilibria combining partial statements with full statements recommending everything. Recommendations in partial statements are always followed; those in full statements are followed probabilistically, leaving senders indifferent. Full statements remain credible despite recommending bad items—what we call credible exaggeration. In experiments, senders use partial statements selectively alongside full statements; receivers follow nearly all recommendations in partial statements and almost half in full statements, transmitting information.
title: Selective Recommendation and Credible Exaggeration in Multidimensional Communication

abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects creative goods markets using data from a large stock images marketplace. In December 2022, the platform announced it would allow artists to sell GenAI-produced images, subject to two conditions: all GenAI images must be labeled, and GenAI would be prohibited in certain markets. We exploit this policy variation using a difference-in-differences design. We estimate a 136% increase in image production and 47% increase in active artists, accompanied by a 15% decline in non-GenAI production and 29% decline in non-GenAI active artists. On the demand side, total sales increase by 82%, but non-GenAI sales fall by 28% and non-GenAI sales rates decline by 3 percentage points. We use image embeddings to develop novel measures of image quality, characteristics, and market composition.We find that quality (measured as predicted sales probability) increases by 9 percentage points overall and 2 percentage points for non-GenAI content, suggesting low-quality non-GenAI artists exit. Our product characteristic measures indicate that GenAI production is heavily concentrated in characteristic space, potentially limiting the value of these images to the market. Non-GenAI production responds to GenAI by differentiating into niches. We discuss implications for copyright policy and the longer-run sustainability of original creative work.
title: Generative AI And Creative Goods: Market Expansion, Crowd-Out, and Copyright

abstract: The rapid expansion of photovoltaic (PV) power stations is essential for achieving carbon neutrality, yet its expanding land footprint may impose negative externalities on ecosystems. Systematic causal evidence on the ecological impacts of large-scale PV expansion, however, remains scarce. A key unresolved question is whether local biodiversity losses near PV stations are offset by gains in surrounding areas. Using bird diversity as an indicator of regional biodiversity, this study integrates satellite-derived PV power station data with citizen science bird observation records from the China Bird Watching Report (CBR) platform, constructing a county-level panel dataset covering 1286 counties over 2015–2024. Employing a two-way fixed effects (TWFE) model combined with a Bartik instrumental variable strategy, this study finds that PV power station expansion significantly reduces county-level species richness and, less robustly, bird abundance, with effects particularly pronounced among resident birds and small-bodied species. Mechanism tests do not support vegetation loss as the channel, and the remaining negative effect is consistent with habitat functional degradation, whereas evidence for a food chain channel is limited and confined mainly to maize. County-level spatial models find no robust spillover to neighboring counties, and a site-level distance-gradient design shows that losses in species richness are concentrated within about 2 km of PV power stations with no detectable compensating gains at greater distances, a pattern more consistent with local loss than with spatial displacement. These findings offer policy implications for reconciling clean energy expansion with biodiversity conservation.

abstract: Governments that rely on a small number of large taxpayers face fiscal risk from the concentration of their revenue base. The granular literature shows that shocks to dominant firms do not wash out in the aggregate, yet their fiscal counterpart is unmeasured. We develop a measure of granular fiscal risk for Macau, where taxes on six casino operators fund most of the government, decomposing operator shocks into sector-wide and firm-specific components weighted by each operator’s contribution to revenue. Sector-wide shocks generate substantial movements in government revenue, the fiscal balance, and aggregate activity, whereas firm-specific shocks primarily affect the volatility of these outcomes. The distinction reflects two dimensions of concentrated fiscal exposure: common shocks determine the level of fiscal outcomes, while idiosyncratic shocks raise their uncertainty. Fiscal dependence on a few large taxpayers thus transmits sectoral and firm-level shocks to public finances, highlighting the stabilizing role of tax-base diversification.
title: Tax-base concentration and granular fiscal risk: Evidence from Macau’s gaming sector

abstract: What determines whether someone complies with a social norm? The social identity approach offers a mechanism for norm compliance: A person who feels similar to a group identifies more with that group and, in turn, complies with the group’s norms. Using an experiment, we test whether similarity in values increases identification and adherence to a group rule. To do so, we varied the similarity/dissimilarity between the values of an individual and members of a social group and measured group identification and rule compliance. We find that moral similarity in progressivism increases group identification, and group identification can increase compliance with rules from the social group. However, our results also suggest that this relationship can be disrupted. Because of our design and empirically verified in our study, social norms do not differ between treatments. As a consequence, observed behavior changes are attributable to increased group norm sensitivity and not changes in group norms. We advance the study of social identity by testing a causal pathway between group identification, group norm sensitivity, and behavior change. Our contribution to the management literature is to extend the empirical rationale, and cautionary notes, for investing in value-alignment between individuals and organizations. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods and the University of Michigan School of Information for financial support. They also gratefully acknowledge support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy (EXC 2126/2 – 390838866), and from the Center for Social and Economic Behavior at the University of Cologne. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08000 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Determinants of Norm Compliance: Moral Similarity and Group Identification

abstract: Institutional investors apply stricter carbon screens abroad than at home. Using global equity holdings for roughly 13,400 institutions across 48 countries over 2005–2024, we show that higher firm emissions predict lower foreign institutional ownership with no corresponding reduction at home; the domestic-foreign ownership gap widens with emissions, and domestic ownership rises with Scope 3 emissions. This carbon home bias remains in within-investor and within-firm comparisons and is not explained by the country-pair determinants of ordinary home bias. It operates through both re-entry (foreign high emitters face a higher hurdle to re-enter a portfolio) and exit (a higher hazard of leaving it). This bias intensified after the Paris Agreement and did not unwind during the subsequent anti-ESG reaction. It is concentrated in discretionary rather than index-constrained holdings; at the extensive margin, the incremental bias is largest among pension funds—institutions particularly associated with formal investment-policy restrictions, and better covered by European than by U.S. filings—rather than among managers best placed to exploit an informational advantage. Overall, the evidence is more consistent with institutional constraints and screening policies than with a simple information-advantage explanation.
title: Carbon home bias

abstract: A worker within a firm, or a researcher within the academia, is required to both cooperate with colleagues in team-projects and to compete with them for career progressions. However, males and females may differently adapt when switching between tasks characterized by different levels of competitiveness and cooperativeness, affecting their labour market outcomes. In this paper we experimentally study individuals’ spillovers of cooperative behaviour when playing indefinitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemmas, distinguished by two different levels of the competitiveness-cooperativeness index ( C C I , Demuynck et al., 2022). Additionally, we investigate whether making the cooperative dimension of the strategic environment more salient affects males’ and females’ behaviour. The analysis is based on 240 participants organized into 24 independent matching groups. Besides supporting the efficacy of the C C I in assessing the competitiveness of an environment, our results provide evidence that females are more likely than males to spill over their cooperative behaviour when switching from a relatively low competitive environment to a relatively high competitive one, informing on how gender diversity within offices might affect individual and organizational outcomes. Finally, our choice architecture intervention is associated with higher cooperation when incentives to cooperate are relatively weak, although this effect does not persist over the entire interaction, while being irrelevant when the context is already favourable to cooperation.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 253
title: Spillover effects of cooperative behaviour when switching tasks: the role of gender

abstract: The separation of the United Kingdom from the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) led to the creation of a national carbon-pricing instrument, the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS), and a corresponding futures market for UK Allowances (UKAs). This study investigates whether this institutional change fragmented liquidity previously concentrated in the European Union Allowance (EUA) futures market. Specifically, we analyse whether trading volume, open interest, bid-ask spreads and the Amihud illiquidity measure shifted following the introduction of the UKA futures market and whether their trajectories subsequently changed. The results indicate a significant deterioration in EUA futures market liquidity following the launch of the UKA futures market reflected in lower trading volume, wider relative spreads and greater price impact, while open interest remained broadly stable.
title: Brexit, liquidity and carbon markets

abstract: Translating global Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) into locally grounded, spatially explicit urban scenarios remains a methodological challenge for urban futures research. This study develops a hybrid framework that combines participatory SSP downscaling, Random Forest-derived urban growth propensity, scenario specific spatial protection, and stochastic cellular automata simulation to examine alternative urban futures for Hue, Vietnam, to 2050. Locally contextualized SSP1–SSP3 assumptions were operationalized through alternative growth settings and protection of ecosystem-based adaptation opportunity areas, flood-prone land, and tourism areas. From a 2020 urban extent of 208.42 km², the mean simulated urban area reached 437.02 km² under SSP1, 487.37 km² under SSP2, and 564.81 km² under SSP3. High probability growth clusters were concentrated in coastal lowlands, peri-urban and industrial development zones, and western development corridors. Agricultural land accounted for the largest share of projected conversion, with combined cropland and rice losses increasing across the scenarios. Landscape analysis indicated increasing urban coalescence in the main simulations; however, a constant area sensitivity showed that part of this pattern resulted from differences in total urban growth quantity. Additional sensitivity experiments confirmed that scenario divergence reflected the combined influence of growth settings and spatial protection. The framework provides a transparent approach for linking locally contextualized SSP narratives with empirical growth patterns, spatial planning constraints, uncertainty, and comparative urban futures analysis.
title: A transferable framework for integrating shared socioeconomic pathways into hybrid urban growth models: Lessons from central Vietnam

abstract: This paper studies how information disclosure affects investment incentives and contracting efficiency. We analyze a class of principal-agent models in which information helps the principal screen the agent but also facilitates surplus appropriation, thereby weakening the agent’s incentive to invest before contracting. Efficient privacy regimes balance these two forces. Along the frontier of efficient information policies, more privacy is associated with stronger investment incentives and higher agent payoff. We characterize conditions under which full privacy, full disclosure, or intermediate privacy is efficient. The results provide guidance for intellectual property and innovation policy by identifying when additional privacy fosters or hinders economic efficiency and innovation. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01507 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Screening, Investment Incentives, and the Welfare Trade-Offs of Privacy

abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?

abstract: Measures of overconfidence are used both to assess biases in people’s beliefs regarding their own abilities and to identify correlates of those biases. Proposed correlates of overconfidence include narcissism, social status, (low) task anxiety, savings, planning, and many more. Research on these correlates typically explicitly or implicitly claims that the associations with overconfidence are not attributable to ability (i.e., latent inputs enabling successful task performance, including inputs that vary across people, states, or contexts). I argue that several typical approaches used to measure overconfidence are not sufficient to support such claims. This argument follows from two underappreciated properties of these measures of overconfidence. First, performance is an imperfect measure of ability: accounting for performance does not sufficiently account for ability. Second, self-evaluations of performance should reflect ability in addition to performance: because performance is ambiguous, people should incorporate prior beliefs about their ability. These properties imply that multiple commonly used measures of overconfidence are confounded with ability. I support these analytical results by reexamining previously published findings. In the first analysis, I find that overconfidence predicts subsequent performance, consistent with measures of overconfidence serving as a signal of ability. In the second set of analyses, I find that some purported associations between overconfidence and other constructs could be attributed to ability instead. I close with recommendations to recognize and reduce the potential for mistaken inferences. When research indicates that differences in overconfidence are associated with other behaviors, beliefs, or evaluations, researchers should account for the possibility that differences in ability could provide a sufficient explanation. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by the UCLA Anderson Morrison Center for Marketing and Data Analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05184 and https://researchbox.org/1597 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Widely Used Measures of Overconfidence Are Confounded with Ability

abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on Italian households’ financial savings and other macroeconomic variables. Unlike previous studies, we identify three distinct shocks: a containment shock, a fear-of-infection shock and an uncertainty shock. To capture their effects and contributions, we employ a time-varying parameter vector autoregression (VAR) model with stochastic volatility. Our findings indicate that the containment shock has a positive and significant impact on household financial savings, whereas the effects of the fear-of-infection and the uncertainty shocks are smaller. Counterfactual exercises suggest that, in the absence of these three shocks, between March and December 2020, financial savings would have been more than 20% lower than the level observed. These results provide new insights into the sources of the rapid accumulation of excess savings and are particularly valuable for policymakers seeking to understand the sharp rise in global inflation following extreme events.
title: Disentangling the effects of COVID-19 induced shocks and uncertainty on households’ financial savings

abstract: Achieving a smooth phase-out and ensuring sustainable development are often the ultimate goals of large-scale anti-poverty programs. We study this transition in the context of China’s 2021 conclusion of its national anti-poverty campaign. Using multi-source data and complementary regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs, we find evidence of a “smooth exit” characterized by an improvement in the mental health and subjective well-being of former beneficiaries following the withdrawal of formal aid. We also find a revitalization of social support during this exit: as the program ceased, material and emotional support from local communities increased and partly substituted for the retracted formal aid. These findings align with a stylized model predicting that post-exit welfare depends on whether the public program strengthened local social capital during its implementation. Our results suggest that investment in local social capital may help sustain well-being after anti-poverty programs end.

abstract: This paper investigates the gender differences in two types of overconfidence: overestimation and overplacement. We aggregate findings from 52 experimental studies in economics, published between 2000-2020—all of which employed real-effort tasks—in a preregistered Bayesian hierarchical analysis. A previous meta-study by Bandiera et al. (2022) concluded that both men and women exhibit overconfidence, with no significant gender differences. However, Moore and Healy (2008) define multiple types of overconfidence, which are sometimes inversely related. Following their terminology, we divide our meta-study sample into two categories—overestimation and overplacement—and test whether the original results still hold. We motivate the division into subsamples with a theoretical argument, which shows that the relationship of the two types of overconfidence is not necessarily fixed. In the overall sample, we find evidence of overconfidence among men and women, with a statistically significant difference in the magnitude of their biases. In the subsamples, we find that both genders exhibit overestimation, with no significant difference between them. However, overplacement is observed among men but not women, resulting in a significant gender gap.
title: Overestimation or overplacement? A meta-study of gender differences in overconfidence

abstract: We experimentally examine variations of a Collective-Risk Social Dilemma (CRSD) to explore how uncertainty about the timing of potential losses affects participants’ contributions to prevent a collective catastrophe. We consider two certainty scenarios concluding at periods 8 and 10, referred to as Certainty 8 and Certainty 10, respectively; a Risk scenario, with the ending period drawn randomly between periods 8 and 12 according to a uniform distribution; and an Ambiguity scenario, with the same possible ending periods, but an unknown probability distribution. We find that average individual contributions under Risk and Ambiguity do not differ significantly from those under Certainty 8, and are significantly higher than those under Certainty 10. Horizon uncertainty encourages early contributions, in contrast to known horizons, where efforts are delayed, and procrastination is observed regardless of the length of the time horizon. However, without sustained contributions, early cooperation alone may not be enough to ensure collective success.
title: Final countdown? An experimental Collective-Risk Social Dilemma with horizon uncertainty

abstract: We study price competition among n firms located on a circle of unit circumference, in the tradition of Salop (1979), when marginal costs differ across firms. The first-order conditions form a circulant linear system. The discrete Fourier transform diagonalises this system, and its inverse turns out to be a real-valued discrete Green’s function G . Equilibrium prices are then simply the cyclic convolution of adjusted costs with G . This closed form recovers, by a different route, the solution of Lin and Wu (2015), and it brings structural rewards of its own. The weights of the convolution measure how strongly each firm’s cost enters each equilibrium price. They are exactly rational for every n , they satisfy simple local identities, and they decay geometrically at the exact rate 2 − 3 , which yields clean pass-through and averaging laws. We then ask when this solution is a genuine Nash equilibrium of the underlying game, in which a firm may also undercut a rival’s delivered price outright. We answer with a closed-form no-undercutting condition, with exact validity thresholds for a single high-cost firm that lie strictly below the demand-positivity threshold, and with the large-market limit ( 6 + 3 ) / ( 11 n ) . Price-based and cost-based validity restrictions turn out to be non-nested. A fully verified numerical example illustrates every step.
title: Closed-form equilibrium prices and Nash validity in the Salop model with heterogeneous costs

abstract: This paper studies a many-to-one matching between individuals and institutions where institutions comprise multiple divisions and face cross-divisional constraints. We introduce a parametrized family of choice rules, which we call generalized sequential (GSq) choice rules, that encompasses many different choice rules encountered in practice and in market design literature. We show that the cumulative offer mechanism (COM) is the unique stable and strategy-proof mechanism in a matching problem where all institutions have a GSq choice rule. The family of GSq choice rules provides a practically communicable representation of complex institutional choice procedures. We present two real-world applications: affirmative action in India’s public school admissions and civil service selection process, and high school admissions in China.

title: Matching with Generalized Sequential Choice Rules

abstract: This paper studies decision problems where the decision maker’s choice of action affects the probability distribution of a payoff relevant random variable. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence of an expected utility maximizing action in such settings. The main requirement is a mild continuity condition on the family of possible distributions. We also show that this condition is a minimal requirement. Our result does not require common assumptions such as the monotone likelihood ratio property (MLRP) or the convexity of distribution functions condition (CDFC). It can therefore be used to prove the existence of an optimal action in many settings where existing results do not apply, including an important class of problems where the support of the random variable depends on the decision maker’s choice and the density functions are not pointwise continuous.
title: Utility maximization under endogenous uncertainty

abstract: We study how public perceptions of monetary policy evolve when the economy experiences rare and severe supply shocks. When agents learn in real time about the distribution of the shocks and the monetary policy reaction function, they tend to underestimate the strength of the response to inflation following large but infrequent negative supply shocks. Embedding this mechanism in a general equilibrium model with learning, we show that it endogenously generates inflation dynamics persistently above target and temporary output overshooting after a tail event. Using U.S. data, we find empirical evidence supporting our model's predictions about the distinctive role of tail events in shaping policy perceptions and macroeconomic dynamics. Our findings indicate that public misperceptions can amplify and prolong the aggregate effects of tail events, potentially undermining central banks' stabilization efforts.
title: When the unthinkable happens: perceptions of monetary policy in tail events

abstract: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)
title: Fintech Expansion

abstract: China's carbon emissions trading system plays a crucial role in achieving national climate goals, yet current carbon emission quota (CEQ) allocation in China's power industry lacks an annual emission cap and overlooks the transfer of carbon emissions from interprovincial power exchanges. This study combines the intergenerational abatement model with the quasi-input-output model to propose a new CEQ allocation strategy that accounts for intergenerational and interprovincial responsibilities for China's power industry. The results show that, when intergenerational equity in emission abatement costs is considered in setting the annual CEQ cap, the increasing emission abatement in China's power industry does not impose a substantial economic burden. Furthermore, incorporating embodied carbon emissions from interprovincial power exchanges into the regional CEQ allocation helps reduce the regional inequities associated with current allocation schemes that rely exclusively on direct emissions. Under the CEQ allocation scheme considering intergenerational and interprovincial responsibilities, economically underdeveloped provinces that are net exporters of power often receive upward adjustments in their allocations and realize abatement cost savings. In contrast, economically developed and net-importing provinces typically experience downward adjustments in their allocations and face higher abatement costs.

title: Carbon emission quota allocation for China's power industry: Considering intergenerational and interprovincial responsibility

abstract: Public acceptance is widely regarded as relevant for the implementation of hydrogen infrastructure, yet existing research has focused mainly on average acceptance levels rather than on how acceptance gaps are distributed within the population. This study empirically examines the gap between national and community acceptance for electrolysers, pipelines, and underground hydrogen storage in Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands, using standardized quota-based online surveys (N = 3402). The results from inferential statistics show robust acceptance gaps across all three technologies, but no substantial differences in gap magnitude between them. Cross-national variation is statistically significant but small. At the individual level, more than half of respondents report identical national and community acceptance ratings, while positive gaps (defined as higher national acceptance than community acceptance) are substantially more common than negative gaps. A descriptive decomposition further shows that respondents meeting a predefined low-community-acceptance threshold account for a disproportionately large share of the aggregate gap. This subgroup is not only less accepting at community level, but also reports substantially lower national acceptance. The findings therefore show that average acceptance ratings alone provide an incomplete basis for interpreting the societal context of hydrogen infrastructure policy, because they may conceal where low acceptance is concentrated within the population. However, the results are to be interpreted with limitations, inter alia because only stated attitudes were measured, rather than actual behaviour.
title: An effect of the few? Public acceptance gaps for hydrogen infrastructure in Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands

abstract: A general equilibrium model of banking and interbank exchange is constructed. The goal is to analyze, in a regime of overnight nominal interest rate targeting, the implications for interest rate control and economic welfare of corridor and floor systems. At the margin, swaps of reserve balances for government debt increase welfare, but above some threshold welfare falls. Critical for the results are bank balance sheet costs associated with regulatory constraints.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
source_issue: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
title: Interest Rate Control and Interbank Markets

abstract: Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2023, this paper measures firm-level artificial intelligence (AI) application through GPT-based semantic analysis of annual reports and constructs a composite index of corporate resilience by combining market stability and financial growth capacity. The empirical results show that AI application significantly enhances corporate resilience, and this finding remains robust across a series of robustness checks. Mechanism analysis indicates that AI application enhances corporate resilience mainly by improving information disclosure quality, reducing transaction costs, and strengthening governance quality. Heterogeneity analysis and external-shock tests further show that the resilience-enhancing effect of AI application is more pronounced in non-technology-intensive industries, regions with lower marketization, and firms with higher ownership concentration; firms with stronger AI capabilities also exhibit greater resilience under extreme weather and energy-constraint shocks. This paper provides new empirical evidence for understanding how AI application strengthens overall corporate resilience.

title: From disruption to adaptation: AI’s pathways to corporate resilience

abstract: Trade between two countries sometimes needs to pass other countries in transit. This applies to landlocked countries and some other overland trade routes. We develop a geography‐based algorithm that identifies, for every country pair, the predicted trade route by road and sea. In a modified gravity model for 1993–2016, trade passing a transit country is roughly half of what it would otherwise be, and the effect weakens when a close alternative route exists – consistent with rent extraction. Embedding transit rents in a general equilibrium framework shows negative welfare effects that extend also beyond countries most directly involved in transit.
title: Assessing the global impact of transit countries in a gravity model

abstract: The growing body of literature on the data economy has focused almost exclusively on consumer data, whose provision is constrained by privacy costs. This paper broadens the scope by introducing two new data types: producer data, which are generated from economic production; and natural data, which can be either collected from nature directly or generated through scientific experiments. We develop a generalized semi‐endogenous growth model that includes all three types of data in a unified framework. Producer data carry no privacy externality, and the provision of these data scales endogenously with output, creating a self‐reinforcing feedback loop between production and innovation. Natural data share the absence of privacy costs but lack this feedback channel, isolating the growth contribution of each property. With the rapid advance of artificial intelligence, synthetic data, a special case of natural data in our framework, may substantially raise the efficiency of data generation, which raises the level of output. If this efficiency keeps improving over time, natural data can also narrow or even reverse the growth‐rate gap with producer data. The three types are combined through a constant elasticity of substitution (CES) aggregator. Their elasticity of substitution acts as a structural switch: as it rises, the economy evolves from a consumer‐data‐dominated stage with relatively low growth to a producer‐data‐dominated stage with higher growth, which describes how the data economy transforms across development stages.
title: From consumption to production: a generalized model of growth for the data economy

abstract: This paper tests the hypothesis that donors rely on their impressions of dictators’ faces to assess their propensity to misuse foreign aid. It examines whether foreign aid is higher in countries ruled by competent-looking or trustworthy-looking dictators. We analyze the relationship between facial impressions and foreign aid on a sample of 274 dictators from 100 nondemocratic countries between 1975 and 2010. We find that the probability of receiving aid is sensitive to dictators’ facial competence, though the amount received is not. We observe that the effect of competence on aid operates primarily through bilateral aid. By contrast, we find no overall evidence that dictators’ facial trustworthiness affects aid. Furthermore, we observe that the impact of facial impressions has evolved over time: trustworthiness was more important to donors during the Cold War, while competence became the most salient trait in the post–Cold War era.
title: Dictator face can aid

abstract: This study examines how India’s 1991 trade liberalisation affected intergenerational educational mobility. We construct a relative rank-based measure of mobility across two generations of the same household from the India Human Development Survey (2011-12) and use district tariff shocks as exogenous variation in trade exposure. Exposure is continuous: the share of an individual’s schooling-continuation years falling after the reform. In a within-district design, a 10-percentage-point tariff cut raises the probability that a household remains in the same educational quintile across generations by 4.1 percentage points at full exposure, against 3.6 under a binary coding. Upward mobility is unaffected. Attainment in years moves by a similar amount but is imprecisely estimated, because the response is concentrated where a year of schooling moves rank most. Tariff cuts fell disproportionately on skill-intensive industries, compressing regional skill premia and household education spending, weakening the incentive for investment that would have changed relative position.
title: Trade Liberalisation and Intergenerational Educational Mobility in India

abstract: Defence budgets are rising across Europe, and several EBRD economies are leading the shift. Whether higher spending supports domestic industry depends on who can supply it. Drawing on the EBRD Transition Report 2026-27, this column shows that emerging Europe’s defence industry combines large, unproductive state-owned incumbents with young defence-tech startups that rarely advance beyond the earliest funding stage. Drones offer an opportunity, but the market for military drones is smaller than the one for commercial drones and supply chains depend heavily on China.
authors: Federica Coelli, Catalina Cozariuc, Anton Grahed

title: Emerging Europe’s defence industrial base: Between legacy firms and new entrants

abstract: Governments are cracking down on hidden fees, expecting all-in prices to sharpen competition and lower what consumers pay. This column studies California’s 2024 requirement that short-term rentals advertise fee-inclusive prices. Guests became more price-sensitive, yet prices rose by about 5%. Consumers still gained on average, largely because the market reshuffled: listings that depended on cleaning fees disproportionately left, higher-quality listings stayed, and cheaper entrants arrived.
authors: Ginger Jin, Liad Wagman, Jingyi Xing
title: When transparency raises prices: Lessons from California’s all-in pricing law for short-term rentals

abstract: What accounts for cross-country heterogeneity in exchange-rate responses to U.S. monetary policy shocks? Using daily data around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announcements for 34 countries from 2001 to 2019, we show that countries with deeper financial markets, measured by foreign portfolio investment liabilities relative to GDP, experience larger short-run currency depreciations following contractionary U.S. monetary policy shocks. This amplification is substantially stronger for forward-guidance shocks than for contemporaneous target-rate surprises. The finding is broadly robust to alternative measures of financial depth and controls for potential confounding factors. In a parsimonious portfolio-adjustment model, greater market depth lowers rebalancing costs, thereby increasing the weight placed on expected future interest-rate differentials and amplifying forward-looking shocks more strongly. A quantitative model–data comparison shows that this mechanism generates a substantial share of the observed asymmetry.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
source_issue: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
title: US Monetary Policy, Exchange Rates, and Delayed Portfolio Adjustments

abstract: We analyze the problem of locating a public facility on a line in a society where agents have either single-peaked or single-dipped preferences. We consider the domain analyzed in Alcalde-Unzu et al. (2024), where the type of preference of each agent is public information, but the location of her peak/dip as well as the rest of the preference are unknown. We characterize all strategy-proof and type-anonymous rules on this domain. Building on existing results, we provide a two-step characterization": first, the median between the peaks and a collection of fixed values is computed (Moulin, 1980), resulting in either a single alternative or a pair of contiguous alternatives. If the outcome of the median is a pair, we apply a double-quota majority method" in the second step to choose between the two alternatives in the pair (Moulin, 1983). We also show the additional conditions that type-anonymity imposes on the strategy-proof rules characterized by Alcalde-Unzu et al. (2024). Finally, we show the equivalence between the two characterizations.
title: Type-anonymity and strategy-proofness in a domain of single-peaked and single-dipped preferences

abstract: This paper studies allocation mechanisms in max-flow games with players' capacities as private information. We first show that no core-selection mechanism is truthful: there may exist a player whose payoff increases if she under-reports her capacity when a core-section mechanism is adopted. We then introduce five desirable properties for mechanisms in max-flow games: DSIC (truthful reporting is a dominant strategy), SIR (individual rationality and positive payoff for each player contributing positively to at least one coalition), SP (no edge has an incentive to split into parallel edges), MP (no parallel edges have incentives to merge), and CM (a player's payoff does not decrease as another player's capacity and max-flow increase). While the Shapley value mechanism satisfies DSIC and SIR, it fails to meet SP, MP and CM. We propose a new mechanism based on minimal cuts that satisfies all five properties.
title: Mechanism design in max-flows with private capacities

abstract: Under differential privacy with global sensitivity, privacy noise in panel data vanishes only with more units behind a coefficient. In a linear panel model with multi-dimensional latent group parameters, the one-dimensional design estimates combinations separately. Sparsity inflates its privacy noise. Under the threat of weak identification, its privacy noise can turn a consistent non-private estimate into an inconsistent private release. The multi-dimensional design pools each coefficient over its group, whose many strongly identified units let the researcher calibrate small privacy noise. At a fixed budget, its releases are N T -asymptotically equivalent to non-private estimates when T / N → 0 .
title: Estimating latent heterogeneity under differential privacy

abstract: Estimating the constraints in the business environment guides development policy and allocation of resources. This paper examines response order bias in survey questions on the biggest obstacle to operations with a lengthy list of response options in the World Bank Enterprise Surveys. Using more than 200,000 interviews with firm managers from 178 economies with randomized response orders, the estimates show that the first three positions have a 9 percent higher relative likelihood of being selected, with the first position on the showcard being 22 percent more likely to be selected. The primacy bias, the tendency to select an early response option, is significantly stronger in low-income economies (17 percent, whereas in high-income economies the bias is statistically nonexistent), creating a troubling paradox: position effects distort estimates most severely where accurate constraint measurement matters most for development policy. Applying empirical Bayes-stabilized inverse probability weights to correct for these biases changes the rank order for 9 percent of the obstacles, affecting about half of the surveys.
journal: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
publisher: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
series: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
source_name: World Bank Policy Research Working Papers
title: First Impressions Matter: Measuring and Correcting Position Bias in Business Environment Estimates

abstract: Socio-emotional skills training is increasingly embedded in youth employment programs, often alongside aspirational content, yet evidence on how these components interact remains limited. This paper evaluates a randomized controlled trial with 6,023 urban out-of-school youth in Côte d'Ivoire. Participants were assigned to a control group or a multi-component employment program whose socio-emotional modules emphasized either intrapersonal or interpersonal skills, and were further randomized to one of two sets of aspirational videos or no video. Impacts differed substantially by gender. For women, both training packages without a video improved labor market participation, and the intrapersonal arm additionally improved sexual and reproductive health, raising contraceptive use and reducing the likelihood of being pregnant or breastfeeding. For most outcomes, equality between the two treatment packages cannot be rejected. For men, the effects were limited. Adding either set of videos largely eliminated women's labor market and reproductive gains, although the videos on shared-responsibilities were also associated with reductions in specific forms of violence among women and with stronger social networks among men. The paper finds little evidence of changes in socio-emotional skills, aspirations, or gender attitudes. Qualitative evidence suggests improvements in confidence, planning, and day-to-day decision-making, while the videos appear to have increased the salience of risks and constraints facing young women. The results suggest that a multi-component skills program can improve women's economic and reproductive outcomes, but also that seemingly complementary motivational content commonly used to reinforce training may erode these gains when increasing the salience of barriers that women remain unable to overcome.

abstract: Using confidential Federal Reserve Discount Window data from March 2023, I study collateral mobility in lender-of-last-resort lending. Banks with prior experience were more likely to post loan collateral and did so two days faster than inexperienced peers, while showing little effect for securities collateral. When loan collateral was pledged to FHLBs, redeployment to the Fed slowed by an additional three to four days, even among sophisticated banks, because of absent subordination agreements and different collateral reporting practices. In fast runs, what matters is not only where collateral sleeps, but how fast it can move when it needs to wake up.
title: Collateral Mobility and the Lender of Last Resort

abstract: Health care utilization per capita varies widely across the United States, yet higher-utilization areas have no better patient health. In the late 2000s, this pattern was widely interpreted as evidence that health care costs could be cut substantially with- out harming patients, which in turn shaped the 2010 Affordable Care Act. We describe how our understanding has since evolved, emphasizing three points. First, new evidence indicates quantitatively meaningful roles for both supply-side and demand-side factors in driving regional variation in health care and in health outcomes. Second, health care productivity varies substantially across providers; improving it requires better understanding of why productivity differs. Third, we know even less about the sources of area-level productivity differences. We suggest several ways in which greater engagement with the productivity literature outside of health care could yield valuable insights.
title: Regional Variations and Productivity Puzzles in Health Care
